title: Optically Active Single Hole Spin in ZnSe
authors: Amirehsan Alizadehherfati, Yuxi Jiang, Kelsey J. Mirrielees, Nils von den Driesch, Christine Falter, Yurii Kutovyi, Amirehsan Boreiri, Douglas L. Irving, Alexander Pawlis, Edo Waks
abstract: Semiconductor hole spins offer a pathway to extended coherence times by decoupling from nuclear magnetic noise, while their spin-orbit coupling enables fast all-electrical control. In ZnSe, however, realizing this potential has been limited by p-doping challenges. Here, we circumvent this limit by optically activating acceptors within the ZnSe quantum well. We isolate a single-hole spin bound to a shallow acceptor, confirmed by antibunching and accessed via the fast (244 ps) radiative recombination of a bound exciton. Magnetic and Raman spectroscopy of the ground state reveal an effective hole g-factor of 0.7 and an optical resonance linewidth of 26.7 GHz. Complementary first-principles simulations, together with the experimental results, provide evidence that points toward nitrogen as the most likely acceptor impurity. These results introduce a promising new platform for optically active spin qubits and single-photon sources in ZnSe.
summary: This paper reports on the successful realization and characterization of optically active single hole spins in ZnSe quantum wells by utilizing acceptor impurities instead of traditional p-doping. By combining DFT calculations, time-resolved spectroscopy, and photon correlation measurements, the authors confirm nitrogen as a promising host impurity for developing solid-state spin qubits and single-photon sources.
main_problem: The goal is to create a promising platform for optically active spin qubits and single-photon sources in ZnSe by overcoming historical p-doping limitations.
main_result: The authors successfully isolated and characterized a single-hole spin bound to an acceptor impurity, identifying nitrogen as the most likely candidate based on spectroscopic and theoretical evidence.
method: A combination of first-principles DFT calculations (to predict defect levels) and advanced optical spectroscopy techniques (PL, time-resolved measurements, magnetospectroscopy) was employed.
model_or_system: The system is a single-hole spin localized at an acceptor impurity within a ZnSe quantum well. The physics involves charge state transitions ($|A^-angle \leftrightarrow |A^0angle$) and the formation of an exciton complex ($|A^0Xangle$).
key_observables: Antibunching ($g^{(2)}(0)$), effective hole g-factor (0.7), optical resonance linewidth ($\approx 26.7 	ext{ GHz}$), and localization energy ($\sim 34 	ext{ meV}$).
important_parameters: Fast radiative recombination lifetime ($\sim 244 	ext{ ps}$); the dependence of emission intensity on above-band vs. resonant pump power.
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes that the observed acceptor state originates from residual nitrogen background rather than intentionally introduced dopants, and that the system can be modeled using steady-state rate equations.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate formation energy comparisons for various impurities; PL spectra show distinct exciton components; time decay fits confirm fast emission lifetimes; and $g^{(2)}(	au)$ measurements demonstrate antibunching.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from identifying the physical challenge (p-doping limitations) to proposing an optical activation method. It then uses DFT calculations to identify the impurity, followed by detailed spectroscopic characterization of the bound exciton and spin properties using time-resolved and magnetic measurements.
why_interesting: This work directly addresses solid-state quantum emitters for qubits. The combination of theoretical defect engineering (DFT) with precise optical characterization of spin states makes it highly relevant to quantum information research in semiconductors.
